step 1 — the two measurements this chain grows from · journal_of_m_com_o10_o15

measurement A o10 · XRD
Milled C10 pattern reproduces the C0 reflections (CeMg12, Y5Mg24, Ce2Mg17, Mg), with only a weak extra Co line (5) at ~44.5 deg
measurement B o15 · TEM:SAED
SAED of milled C10: rings indexed Ce2Mg17 (306), Co (111), Y5Mg24 (330), CeMg12 (202)

What does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/phase/identity, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?

what step 1 concluded

XRD (bulk powder pattern) and TEM/SAED (local nanoscale diffraction) independently index the same set of phases in milled C10 -- CeMg12, Y5Mg24, Ce2Mg17, Mg from XRD, and Ce2Mg17, Co, Y5Mg24, CeMg12 from SAED rings -- and the weak extra XRD line at ~44.5 deg is corroborated as a distinct Co phase by the separate Co (111) SAED ring. Together, a bulk-averaged technique and a local, spatially-resolved technique agree that Co appears only as its own separate crystalline phase alongside the unchanged C0 alloy phases, with no new reflections or rings indicating a Co-alloy reaction product. Cross-validation across the two techniques makes the 'Co stays a distinct phase, no new phase formed' reading more secure than either pattern would support alone.
Neither technique nor their combination reports on chemical bonding, interdiffusion below diffraction detectability, or amorphous/interfacial reaction layers that would not produce a distinct new reflection or ring
SAED is from a small selected area and is not shown to be representative of the whole milled powder, while XRD is bulk-averaged and may not detect a highly dispersed or minor reaction product; combining them does not by itself prove the whole sample is free of any localized reaction, only that neither method finds evidence of one
The weak Co XRD line (5) is a single, faint reflection near 44.5 deg; the pairing corroborates its assignment to Co but does not by itself quantify the amount, distribution, or particle size of Co
This pair covers only the milled C10 state; it says nothing about phase/identity behavior after de/hydrogenation cycling

new measurement o28
PCT at 320-360 C: one flat plateau per temperature; C10 plateaus lie at nearly the same pressures as C0 (~0.15, 0.27, 0.45 MPa)

What does this measurement, read together with the established earlier result below, settle about PRP/value that neither settles on its own? Say what the combination supports and what it leaves open.

what this step concluded

Read together, the phase-identity finding (Co remains only a separate, unreacted crystalline phase alongside the unchanged C0 phases in milled C10, with no new Co-alloy reflections/rings) and the PCT finding (C10 plateau pressures at 320-360 C fall at nearly the same values as C0, ~0.15, 0.27, 0.45 MPa) are mutually consistent across two independent measurement domains: structural and thermodynamic. Neither alone would show this consistency -- the phase data say nothing about hydrogen equilibrium behavior, and the matching plateaus alone would not indicate whether the match reflects true structural non-interaction or is coincidental. Together they support that Co, present only as a segregated additive phase, does not perturb the intrinsic hydrogen-equilibrium thermodynamics of the host Mg-alloy phases in the milled (pre-cycling) state.
Plateau pressure is an equilibrium/thermodynamic quantity, not a kinetic one; the pair says nothing about absorption/desorption rates or any catalytic effect Co might have, which is a different kind of question from thermodynamics
Per the qualifications on the phase-identity result, undetected interdiffusion, amorphous interfacial layers, or highly dispersed/minor reaction product could exist without producing a new reflection/ring and without necessarily shifting a bulk plateau pressure detectably -- the combination cannot rule this out, only note that neither method found evidence of it
Only three (temperature, pressure) points are compared (320-360 C against ~0.15, 0.27, 0.45 MPa); this is too few to establish a full thermodynamic equivalence, only a rough match at those points
The phase-identity result is stated only for the milled C10 state (not after de/hydrogenation cycling), so the combined claim likewise applies only to that pre-cycling condition and says nothing about phase or thermodynamic behavior after cycling

the chain read straight through

The chain starts with two diffraction measurements on milled C10: bulk XRD shows the normal C0 reflections (CeMg12, Y5Mg24, Ce2Mg17, Mg) plus one weak extra line near 44.5 degrees, while local TEM/SAED shows rings indexing the same host phases plus a separate Co ring. Neither reading alone would settle whether that weak XRD line was a real, distinct Co phase: XRD is bulk-averaged and the line is faint, and SAED is only local. Put together, the two techniques cross-validate each other, so step 1 concludes Co sits as its own separate crystalline phase next to the unchanged C0 phases, with no new reaction product. Step 2 then adds PCT curves at 320-360 C, where C10 plateau pressures (~0.15, 0.27, 0.45 MPa) nearly match C0. This measurement needed the step 1 result because PCT alone is a thermodynamic, not structural, reading -- a plateau match could be coincidental without knowing what phases are actually present. Knowing Co is a segregated, unreacted phase lets the matching plateaus be read as showing that segregated Co does not perturb the host alloy's hydrogen-equilibrium thermodynamics, at least in the milled, pre-cycling state, and only regarding equilibrium pressure rather than kinetics.

step 1 — the two measurements this chain grows from · journal_of_m_com_o12_o18

measurement A o12 · XRD
Dehydrogenated C0 and C10: Mg, CeH2.73, CeO2, YH2 reflections, no CeMg12/Y5Mg24/Ce2Mg17; Co marker at ~44.5 deg in C10
measurement B o18 · TEM:HRTEM
HRTEM of dehydrogenated C10: Mg (101) 0.245 nm grain wrapped by carbon layers beside a CeH2.73 (111) 0.318 nm grain

What does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/phase/identity, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?

what step 1 concluded

XRD establishes, across the bulk of the dehydrogenated sample, that only Mg, CeH2.73, CeO2 and YH2 reflections are present (with a Co marker peak in C10) and that no CeMg12/Y5Mg24/Ce2Mg17 reflections appear, i.e. no RE-Mg intermetallic phase forms anywhere detectable in the bulk. HRTEM then shows, at one imaged region of dehydrogenated C10, a real-space grain with 0.245 nm spacing matching Mg (101) sitting directly beside a grain with 0.318 nm spacing matching CeH2.73 (111), with the Mg grain wrapped by carbon layers. Put together, the local lattice-resolved image corroborates that the phases XRD assigns bulk-wide (Mg, CeH2.73) are genuinely present as distinct, physically adjacent crystalline grains rather than an XRD artifact, and adds real-space morphological information -- the carbon wrapping of the Mg grain -- that diffraction alone cannot supply.
XRD alone gives bulk-averaged phase presence/absence but no information on spatial arrangement, grain morphology, or whether phases are adjacent/wrapped by carbon
HRTEM alone images only one local grain pair and cannot establish that this Mg/CeH2.73 adjacency or the absence of RE-Mg phases is representative of the whole sample
the pairing does not by itself establish reversibility or cycling behavior -- only phase identity and local morphology in the dehydrogenated state shown in these panels
what travelled into step 2

XRD establishes, across the bulk of the dehydrogenated sample, that only Mg, CeH2.73, CeO2 and YH2 reflections are present (with a Co marker peak in C10) and that no CeMg12/Y5Mg24/Ce2Mg17 reflections appear, i.e. no RE-Mg intermetallic phase forms anywhere detectable in the bulk. HRTEM then shows, at one imaged region of dehydrogenated C10, a real-space grain with 0.245 nm spacing matching Mg (101) sitting directly beside a grain with 0.318 nm spacing matching CeH2.73 (111), with the Mg grain wrapped by carbon layers. Put together, the local lattice-resolved image corroborates that the phases XRD assigns bulk-wide (Mg, CeH2.73) are genuinely present as distinct, physically adjacent crystalline grains rather than an XRD artifact, and adds real-space morphological information -- the carbon wrapping of the Mg grain -- that diffraction alone cannot supply.

the chain read straight through

Bulk XRD on the dehydrogenated C0 and C10 samples finds only Mg, CeH2.73, CeO2 and YH2 reflections (plus a Co marker peak in C10), with no CeMg12/Y5Mg24/Ce2Mg17 lines anywhere detectable, establishing the phase assemblage and ruling out any RE-Mg intermetallic in the bulk. This combined phase/morphology result was then handed to the PCT plateau measurement at 320-360 C, which shows one flat plateau per temperature with C10 sitting at nearly the same pressures as C0 (~0.15, 0.27, 0.45 MPa). The pressure data alone say nothing about phase identity, so only paired with the prior result can one read the unchanged plateaus as consistent with no new phase forming, supporting that C@Co treatment and cycling leave both the phase assemblage and the desorption thermodynamics essentially unchanged -- while kinetics, reversibility across cycles, and how representative the single HRTEM grain pair is remain unaddressed.

new measurement o20
Second (diffusion-controlled) absorption stage lasts 66 min for C0 and 11 min for C10 at 360 C

What does this measurement, read together with the established earlier result below, settle about PRP/value that neither settles on its own? Say what the combination supports and what it leaves open.

what this step concluded

Read together, the structural corroboration that a curved-carbon phase coats the alloy particle surface at particle edges (established via EDS+HRTEM) and the kinetic finding that the diffusion-controlled second absorption stage finishes far faster in C10 (11 min) than in C0 (66 min) at 360 C jointly support a plausible structure-to-kinetics correspondence: the carbon coating sits exactly where diffusion into/through the particle would occur, so its presence is spatially consistent with, and could plausibly contribute to, the markedly shortened diffusion-controlled stage seen in the carbon-coated sample. Neither piece alone supports this link -- the structural result (A) says nothing about absorption timing, and the kinetic result (B) says nothing about where or what carbon phase is present.
The HRTEM basis for the structural side is a single local edge region of one milled C10 particle, not shown representative of every surface where carbon sits, so the 'coating explains faster diffusion' picture rests on one local observation, not a particle-wide structural survey
EDS's coarse areal resolution versus HRTEM's atomic resolution means the location pairing is only qualitative, so it cannot be tied quantitatively to the 66 min vs 11 min timing difference
No Co-containing lattice fringe is reported alongside the carbon layers, so the combination does not show Co dispersed atomically within/near the carbon in a way that could mechanistically explain the diffusion speed-up -- only that C and Co signals co-locate at the coarser EDS scale
The two observations are different kinds of quantity: A is a qualitative structural/spatial description (lattice-fringe spacings, edge location) with no rate or time attached, while B is a single-temperature timing measurement (duration in minutes at 360 C) with no structural content -- there is no shared quantitative axis linking them, only a narrative correspondence
Only two time values at one temperature (66 min for C0, 11 min for C10 at 360 C) are available, which supports an ordering (C10 faster) but not a dose-response or mechanistic relationship between amount/location of carbon and diffusion time
B's 360 C diffusion-stage timing is a different metric and temperature window from the paper's headline R10min comparison at 250-100 C, so this combination does not extend to or confirm that separate claim

the chain read straight through

The chain starts from two measurements taken together. The EDS map shows C and Co signals concentrated on particle surfaces, densest along edges and some faces, telling us where these elements sit at the particle scale but nothing about their atomic-scale form. The HRTEM image of milled C10 then zooms into one such edge and shows crystalline CeMg12 (0.258 nm) and Y5Mg24 (0.265 nm) alloy fringes next to an amorphous band and curved carbon layers (0.386 nm), giving atomic-resolution content but only for one local spot. Combined, they support that the C-rich EDS surface signal corresponds to an actual curved-carbon phase coating the alloy particle at its edges, next to alloy grains -- neither measurement alone establishes this, since EDS lacks atomic detail and HRTEM lacks particle-wide spatial context. Step 2 then adds the kinetic measurement that the diffusion-controlled second absorption stage lasts 66 min for C0 versus 11 min for C10 at 360 C. Needing the structural result to interpret it, this timing is read alongside the carbon-coating finding to suggest the coating's location matches where diffusion would occur, making it spatially consistent with the faster C10 kinetics, though not proven to cause it, since the structural evidence is one local observation and the timing is only two values at one temperature.

what this step concluded

Read together, the microstructural corroboration (carbon curved-layer phase confirmed at alloy particle edges in C10, per EDS+HRTEM) and the JMAK kinetic result (eta falls from 1.59 in C0 to 1.32 in C10, both fits linear with R2>0.98) support the idea that the carbon phase associated with C10 processing coincides with a change in the apparent nucleation/growth character of the desorption transformation -- i.e., the presence of the surface carbon layer in C10 tracks with a lower Avrami exponent than the carbon-free C0 case. Neither piece alone supports this: the HRTEM/EDS result by itself says nothing about desorption kinetics, and the JMAK eta values by themselves say nothing about what physical feature in C10 differs from C0.
The comparison is only two samples (C0 vs C10), so it establishes an ordering (eta lower where carbon phase is documented) but not a dose-response or statistically robust relationship between carbon coating and eta.

The two observations are different kinds of evidence (structural/spatial identification vs. a kinetic exponent from bulk desorption data) and are not connected by any stated model translating carbon-layer location into an expected eta value; the pairing therefore corroborates a qualitative association, not a quantified mechanistic link.

7step 2No Co-containing lattice fringe was reported in the HRTEM data, so the combination says nothing about how (or whether) Co dispersion contributes to the kinetic change; only the carbon phase's presence/location is corroborated.respectsthe presence of the surface carbon layer in C10 tracks with a lower Avrami exponent
Attributes the tracked feature to the carbon phase only, making no claim about Co dispersion's role in the kinetic change.
8step 2C10 processing (milling with carbon) inherently changes more than carbon content -- e.g., particle/grain refinement from milling -- and the carbon phase and any such refinement occur together by construction in the same sample, so the pair cannot attribute the eta decrease specifically to the carbon coating as opposed to other co-occurring milling effects.ignoresthe presence of the surface carbon layer in C10 tracks with a lower Avrami exponent than the carbon-free C0 case
Singles out the carbon layer as the tracked feature without acknowledging that co-occurring milling effects (e.g., grain refinement) could equally explain the eta change.
